awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Novel Statistical Framework for Validating Large Language Model Outputs
awd_abstract_narration:
The significance of this I-Corps project is based on the translation from lab to market of a new method for validating artificial intelligence (AI) outputs that will help industries adopt trustworthy and reliable AI technologies. The solution generates calibrated confidence scores, indicating when decision-makers can rely on AI outputs. The fundamental issue this solution seeks to address is how to ensure AI produces trustworthy responses when used in industry applications, making it safer and more practical to use AI systems across different industries. The potential impact of commercializing this technology is more widespread adoption of AI tools in critical situations, enabling decision-makers to act more confidently, especially when time is critical. By bringing this advance to the marketplace, the gap between AI's potential and its real-world use could be bridged, helping ensure U.S. dominance in the AI industry worldwide.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a novel statistical framework for validating Large Language Model (LLM) outputs in settings where traditional benchmarking is impossible or unreliable due to the lack of data or the presence of human disagreement. The solution employs advanced statistical techniques to quantify uncertainty in AI-generated responses by analyzing patterns of agreement and disagreement between multiple model runs and between models and human experts. The approach differs from traditional model validation methods that require a gold standard for comparison and only offer an average accuracy level, instead of being individualized to the exact output. By generating calibrated confidence scores that correlate with accuracy, the technology enables users to make informed decisions about when to trust AI outputs, even in high-stakes domains requiring significant human judgment like healthcare and finance.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The goal of this I-Corps project was to test whether a new statistical approach for checking the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence could be turned into a useful product. Large language models can now read scientific documents and pull out information far faster than a person can, but they sometimes make mistakes, and there has been no reliable way to know when their output can be trusted and when it cannot. The statistical framework measures the reliability of an automated reading of a document, a way to tell the difference between an AI that solved for the answer and one that is guessing. Our aim during this award was to learn whether, and for whom, this capability solves a real problem worth paying for.
To answer that, the team conducted 111 customer-discovery interviews with potential users and experts around the world, in North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. We began with a specific bet: that pharmaceutical companies would want fast, high-quality systematic reviews of the scientific literature — the large evidence summaries used in clinical trial design, market access, and drug-safety monitoring — backed by validated AI output. The existing market for this work is substantial, with individual reviews often costing well over one hundred thousand dollars.

What we heard repeatedly reshaped the plan. Customers told us they did not want the entire review process automated; they wanted one painful part of it solved well. Again and again, scientists described spending enormous amounts of time pulling numbers and findings out of published papers, only to discover that the papers contained errors, were internally inconsistent, used non-standard measures, or were formatted in ways that made analysis difficult. The deepest and most common pain was not writing the review — it was getting clean, trustworthy, analysis-ready data out of messy documents.

This insight led the team to pivot. Rather than offering a complete systematic-review service, we refocused on extracting high-quality, validated, analysis-ready data from scientific documents and delivering it as a service, with our statistical validation framework providing the assurance that the extracted information is correct. This narrower offering matched a clearer and more urgent need, particularly among data scientists who rely on such information for research and business decisions.

The principal outcome of the award was a validated decision to move toward commercialization. The team determined that the strongest near-term market lies with customers who feel this pain acutely but do not require the heaviest levels of regulatory validation, and resolved to build an early version of the product, pursue pilot projects suggested by interviewees, and pursue follow-on funding mechanisms, such as the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR/STTR) program, to retire the remaining technical risk in validating AI-generated output. This work is being carried forward through a new venture, Rohe Nordberg Review.

The intellectual merit of the project lies in connecting a rigorous statistical method for quantifying the reliability of automated document reading to a concrete, real-world need, and in sharpening, through direct contact with users, the questions the underlying research must answer.

The broader impacts are twofold. First, tools that make AI-extracted scientific information demonstrably trustworthy can improve the integrity, speed, and reproducibility of the evidence used in medicine, public health, and regulatory decisions that affect many people. Second, the project provided intensive entrepreneurial training: the Entrepreneurial Lead, statistics PhD student Auden Nordberg Krauska, gained hands-on experience translating research into practice, and the Principal Investigator gained direct experience moving an academic idea toward a product — strengthening the pipeline from publicly funded research to public benefit.
